questions.topic: What the moment of inertia measures
questions.learningObjective: State what the moment of inertia measures about a chosen axis
questions.stem: The plotted inertia curve asks which quantity the moment of inertia describes; which statement is right?

options.text: It measures how strongly the body's mass resists changes in its rotation about a chosen axis.
It measures the turning effect of a force applied about a chosen pivot point.
options.misconception: confuses the moment of inertia with torque

options.text: It measures the fraction of the body's mass that lies within the chosen axis.
options.misconception: believes the moment of inertia counts the mass near the axis

options.text: It measures the body's resistance to sliding motion along a flat surface.
options.misconception: confuses rotational inertia with friction on a surface

questions.explanation: The moment of inertia sums m r squared over the body about a chosen axis, so it measures how much mass sits how far from that axis. Torque is the turning effect of a force, not the inertia.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What the moment of inertia measures
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the moment of inertia measures and why it acts like a mass
questions.stem: The disk comparison plot compares two bodies of equal mass with their mass placed differently; what does the moment of inertia measure, and why?

answer.exemplar: The moment of inertia of a body about an axis is the sum of mass times distance squared for every piece of the body, so it measures how the mass is spread about that axis. A body with the same total mass but its mass held further from the axis resists angular acceleration more strongly, just as a heavier mass resists linear acceleration. That is why it is often called the rotational mass of the body, and why every rotational calculation needs the axis stated.

questions.explanation: The moment of inertia sums mass times distance squared about a chosen axis, so it captures both the amount of mass and its distance from the axis. That is why it plays the part of a mass in the rotational equations.
questions.hint: Mass times distance squared, summed over the body.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a torque measures about a chosen pivot
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the same force can give different torques on different rigs
questions.stem: The rolling torque graph evaluates why the same force can give different torques on two rigs; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Torque is the turning effect of a force about a chosen pivot, and it is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. The same push on a short arm and on a long arm therefore gives different torques, and the same force applied at a different angle changes the perpendicular component and so the torque as well. Changing the pivot to a different point changes the lever arm and changes the torque again.

questions.explanation: Torque depends on the force and on the perpendicular lever arm about the chosen pivot, so the same force can turn one rig more than another. Changing the pivot or the pull angle changes that arm.
questions.hint: Torque depends on the lever arm about the pivot.

questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a uniform rod about its centre
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rod's inertia differs between centre and end axes
questions.stem: A rod inertia graph evaluates why a uniform rod has a much smaller inertia about its centre than about one end. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: For a uniform rod of mass m and length L the moment of inertia about its centre is m L squared over twelve, while about one end it is m L squared over three, four times larger. The reason is the distribution of the mass relative to the axis. About the centre the two halves of the rod sit at small distances on average, while about the end every piece lies at a distance between zero and the full length, so squaring the distances lifts the total.

questions.explanation: About the centre the rod's mass lies close to the axis on average, while about the end it lies at distances up to the full length and squaring the distances lifts the total. The end value is four times the centre value.
questions.hint: Compare where the mass sits relative to each axis.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What the moment of inertia measures
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a hoop spins up more slowly than a disk
questions.stem: The disk comparison plot compares how a hoop and a disk spin up under the same torque; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: For a given torque the angular acceleration equals the torque divided by the moment of inertia, so the body with the larger inertia gains angular speed more slowly. A thin hoop places all of its mass at the full radius and has an inertia of m R squared, while a solid disk of the same mass and radius spreads its mass through the interior and gives half that value. The hoop therefore resists angular acceleration roughly twice as strongly, and reaches a given angular speed later.

questions.explanation: Angular acceleration is torque divided by moment of inertia, and the hoop's mass at the full radius gives it twice the disk's value for the same mass and radius, so the same torque spins it up more slowly.
questions.hint: The larger inertia means the smaller angular acceleration.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a torque measures about a chosen pivot
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a torque must be quoted about a stated pivot
questions.stem: A rolling torque graph evaluates why a torque must always be quoted about a stated pivot; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A torque measures the turning effect of a force, and the size of that effect depends on where the body is held, because the lever arm is measured from the pivot to the line of action of the force. The same push on the same rod can therefore be a large torque about a pivot at one end and a small torque about a pivot near the middle. Quoting a torque without the pivot makes the number meaningless, and a graph of torque against angle must say which pivot it used.

questions.explanation: The lever arm is measured from the pivot to the line of the force, so the same force gives different torques about different pivots. A torque quoted without its pivot cannot be compared with anything.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a narrow-base stand tips when the weight acts outside the base
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the restoring moment of a heavy machine about its tipping edge
questions.stem: The pivot weight chart tracks a 200 kg machine whose base is 1.5 m wide; what restoring moment about the tipping edge does its own weight give, in newton metres?
questions.explanation: The machine's weight acts at the centre of its base, 0.75 m from the tipping edge, so the restoring moment is 200 x 9.81 x 0.75 = 1471.5 N m. Using the full 1.5 m base would double it wrongly.
questions.hint: The weight acts at the centre of the base.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a thin hoop about its central axis
questions.learningObjective: Apply the hoop formula for a moment of inertia
questions.stem: An engineering torque plot asks for the moment of inertia of a 6.0 kg hoop of radius 0.35 m about its central axis, in kg m^2.
questions.explanation: A hoop has all its mass at the radius, so the inertia about the central axis is m R squared, 6.0 x 0.1225 = 0.735 kg m^2. A solid disk of the same mass and radius would give half this.
questions.hint: Use mass times radius squared for a hoop.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Torque of an angled force applied to a rod on a pivot
questions.learningObjective: Find the torque of an angled pull and identify the term used
questions.stem: The spin angle graph compares a 2.5 m arm pulled by 50 N at 30 degrees; first find the torque, then say which term gives it.

options.text: The torque is 125 N m, using the full force and the full arm.
options.misconception: ignores the angle in the turning component

options.text: The torque is 62.5 N m, and it comes from the component along the arm.
options.misconception: credits the along-arm component for the turning

options.text: The torque is 62.5 N m, and it comes from the component perpendicular to the arm.
The torque is 31.25 N m, and it comes from halving the perpendicular component.
options.misconception: halves the perpendicular component for no stated reason

questions.explanation: The perpendicular component of the 50 N pull is 50 N times sin 30 degrees, which is 25 N, and over the 2.5 m arm that gives 62.5 N m. The component along the arm produces no turning at all.
questions.hint: Only the perpendicular component turns the arm.
